title: Barbourville, the Knox County seat on the Cumberland
summary: Knox County was formed on December 19, 1799, and James Barbour’s offer of land broke a tied court in 1800; the town on the Cumberland took his name.
bodyMarkdown:
Barbourville sits in the valley of the upper Cumberland River where Richland Creek comes in, near the middle of Knox County. It began as a bargain struck to break a deadlocked county court.

## A new county

The General Assembly [created Knox County on December 19, 1799](https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1385&context=kentucky_county_histories), carving it entirely out of Lincoln County. It was Kentucky’s forty-first county, and at first it took in some 2,300 square miles of the upper Cumberland country; Clay, Rockcastle, Whitley, Harlan, Laurel and Bell counties were later cut from it until it shrank to 388. The name is usually credited to [Henry Knox](https://grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Knox), Washington’s artillery chief and first secretary of war, though some twentieth-century historians argued for the long hunter [James Knox](/stories/james-knox/), who sat in the state senate for Lincoln County when the county was formed.

## A gift with conditions

A county needed a seat. When the new magistrates met in the fall of 1800, they [split three to three](https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/rennick_ms_collection/87) between Flat Lick and a site near the mouth of Richland Creek. James Barbour, a Virginia-born settler who owned some 5,000 acres there, broke the tie. He offered [two acres outright for a public square](https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/NRHP/84003885_text) and 36 more to be laid off in town lots, with the money from the lots divided between the county and himself. The court accepted, and the town took his name.

The plan was a two-acre court square ringed by lots of similar size. Lots were advertised in the middle of 1802. Lot No. 1 sold to Richardson Herndon for $16, and most of the lots around the square were gone by the end of 1803.

The town grew up near Richard Ballinger’s tavern, a known stop on the [Wilderness Road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wilderness_Road), and its post office opened on April 1, 1804. In 1800 the whole county [counted 1,109 people](https://nkaa.uky.edu/nkaa/items/show/2409), 62 of them enslaved.

## Older footprints, slow growth

The ground had a longer story. In April 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker’s exploring party raised a small log cabin a few miles away, and a [state marker for that first cabin](https://history.ky.gov/markers/first-cabin-in-kentucky) stands in town; his journey is told in the [Cumberland Gap story](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/). Growth came slowly. By 1840 Barbourville had [224 residents](https://grokipedia.com/page/Barbourville,_Kentucky), five stores and groceries, a tavern, three churches, a school and the courthouse.

## The fight at the bridge

The Civil War arrived early. Through the summer of 1861 Unionists from Kentucky and East Tennessee drilled at Camp Andrew Johnson near town. On the foggy morning of [September 19, 1861](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Barbourville), about 800 Confederates under Col. Joel A. Battle, sent by Gen. [Felix Zollicoffer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Felix_Zollicoffer), came up from Cumberland Ford. Most of the recruits had already gone to Camp Dick Robinson.

About 300 Home Guards under Capt. Isaac J. Black pulled the planks off the bridge and held the crossing until they were driven off. It was the [first skirmish in eastern Kentucky](https://history.ky.gov/markers/civil-war-actions) and is counted as the first Confederate victory in the state. A month later the campaign was checked at [Camp Wildcat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Camp_Wildcat).

## Kentucky today

[Union College](https://history.ky.gov/markers/union-college), incorporated in 1879, carries on as Union Commonwealth University. The county courthouse stands on the square James Barbour gave, where the map pin sits, and markers for the 1861 fight stand in the town’s Civil War park.
